# Firstlight UI Documentation

> Build a standard NativePHP forms app, by hand or with a coding agent, from genuine SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose controls, Laravel validation, and tested recipes.

--- Source: docs/how-to/build-a-list-detail-flow.md ---

# Build a List and Detail Flow

This recipe gives an app its shell: a layout with the platform's own title bar
and back navigation, a list screen, and a detail screen it pushes. Every other
recipe runs inside this layout.

This recipe runs unchanged in the
[showcase app](https://github.com/firstlightui/showcase), where
[`ListDetailRecipeTest`](https://github.com/firstlightui/showcase/blob/main/tests/Feature/Recipes/ListDetailRecipeTest.php)
exercises it.

Firstlight does not draw navigation. NativePHP Mobile renders it natively when
a layout opts in with `usesNativeChrome()`:

| Behaviour | iOS | Android |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stack | SwiftUI `NavigationStack` | Material 3 `Scaffold` |
| Title | Large title that collapses to inline on scroll | `LargeTopAppBar` / `TopAppBar` |
| Back | System back button and edge swipe | Top app bar back arrow and system back |

PHP stays in charge of the screen stack. A back swipe or back press pops PHP's
stack, so `mount()` and screen state behave the same on both platforms.

## 1. Write the layout

Save this as `app/NativeComponents/Layouts/AppLayout.php`:

```php
<?php

namespace App\NativeComponents\Layouts;

use FirstlightUI\NativeComponent as FirstlightScreen;
use Native\Mobile\Edge\Layouts\Builders\NavBar;
use Native\Mobile\Edge\Layouts\NativeLayout;
use Native\Mobile\Edge\NativeComponent;

class AppLayout extends NativeLayout
{
    public function usesNativeChrome(): bool
    {
        return true;
    }

    public function navBar(NativeComponent $screen): ?NavBar
    {
        $isRoot = $screen instanceof FirstlightScreen && $screen->isRootScreen();

        return NavBar::make()
            ->title($screen->navTitle())
            ->displayMode($isRoot ? 'large' : 'inline')
            ->back(! $isRoot);
    }
}
```

`isRootScreen()` is true when nothing is below the screen on PHP's stack. The
first screen gets a large title and no back button; every pushed screen gets an
inline title and a back button. Android shows a back arrow only when the bar
asks for one, so pushed screens must pass `back(true)`. Each screen supplies its
title through `navTitle()`.

## 2. Register the routes

```php
use App\NativeComponents\Layouts\AppLayout;
use App\NativeComponents\PostScreen;
use App\NativeComponents\PostsScreen;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::native('/posts', PostsScreen::class)->layout(AppLayout::class);
Route::native('/posts/{post}', PostScreen::class)->layout(AppLayout::class);
```

## 3. Write the list screen

Use the [searchable list recipe](build-a-searchable-list-screen.md). Its row
press pushes the detail screen:

```php
public function openPost(int $id): void
{
    $this->navigate('/posts/'.$id);
}
```

`navigate()` pushes. Use `replace()` to swap the current screen without adding
to the stack, and `back()` to pop it from PHP, for example after saving.

## 4. Write the detail screen

```php
<?php

namespace App\NativeComponents;

use App\Models\Post;
use FirstlightUI\NativeComponent;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class PostScreen extends NativeComponent
{
    public Post $post;

    public function navTitle(): string
    {
        return $this->post->title;
    }

    public function render(): View
    {
        return view('native.post');
    }
}
```

NativePHP fills a typed public property from the route parameter with the same
name, using Laravel route model binding: `{post}` becomes a `Post` loaded by id.
No `mount()` is needed.

Save the view as `resources/views/native/post.blade.php`:

```blade
<native:scroll-view class="w-full flex-1">
    <native:column class="w-full p-4 gap-3">
        <native:text class="text-sm text-theme-on-surface-variant">{{ $post->created_at->diffForHumans() }}</native:text>
        <native:text class="text-base text-theme-on-surface">{{ $post->body }}</native:text>
    </native:column>
</native:scroll-view>
```

## Rules to keep

- Return `true` from `usesNativeChrome()`. Without it, NativePHP falls back to
  drawn bars that do not support large titles or the iOS back swipe.
- Do not add the `custom` attribute to `<native:top-bar>` or
  `<native:bottom-nav>`. It keeps the drawn bar.
- Pass stable ids in URLs, never list positions.
- Let the platform draw the back button. Do not add your own back Button.

## Known limits

- Tabs added with `tabBar()` share PHP's single stack. Switching tabs replaces
  the screen, so each tab does not keep its own history.
- Android receives back only when the gesture completes. It does not show the
  predictive-back preview while the user drags.

--- Source: docs/how-to/build-a-searchable-list-screen.md ---

# Build a Searchable List Screen

This recipe builds the index screen most apps need: a search field above a
list of records, with pull-to-refresh, infinite scrolling, a tap that opens
the record, and a swipe action that deletes it after native confirmation.

This recipe runs unchanged in the
[showcase app](https://github.com/firstlightui/showcase), where
[`SearchableListRecipeTest`](https://github.com/firstlightui/showcase/blob/main/tests/Feature/Recipes/SearchableListRecipeTest.php)
exercises it.

Use it when a screen shows many records of one model and the user needs to
find, open, or remove one. Use [List](../components/list.md) without search for
short, fixed collections, and a settings layout when rows change preferences
instead of opening records.

Every piece is an existing Firstlight tag or `NativeComponent` helper. There is
no list-screen tag to learn.

## 1. Register the route

```php
use App\NativeComponents\Layouts\AppLayout;
use App\NativeComponents\PostsScreen;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::native('/posts', PostsScreen::class)
    ->name('posts')
    ->layout(AppLayout::class);
```

`AppLayout` gives the screen a native title bar and back navigation. It is
defined in [Build a list and detail flow](build-a-list-detail-flow.md).

## 2. Write the screen

Extend `FirstlightUI\NativeComponent`. It already includes
[PaginatesLists](paginate-lists.md), [DestroysListItems](destroy-list-items.md),
and [AuthorizesActions](authorize-actions.md).

```php
<?php

namespace App\NativeComponents;

use App\Models\Post;
use FirstlightUI\NativeComponent;
use FirstlightUI\Pagination\ListPage;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class PostsScreen extends NativeComponent
{
    public string $query = '';

    public function mount(): void
    {
        $this->reload();
    }

    public function updatedQuery(): void
    {
        $this->reload();
    }

    public function reload(): void
    {
        $this->refreshList(fn (ListPage $page) => $this->posts($page));
    }

    public function loadMore(): void
    {
        $this->loadMoreList(fn (ListPage $page) => $this->posts($page));
    }

    public function openPost(int $id): void
    {
        $this->navigate('/posts/'.$id);
    }

    public function requestDeletion(int $id): void
    {
        $this->requestDestructiveListAction($id, 'delete');
    }

    public function cancelDeletion(): void
    {
        $this->cancelDestructiveListAction();
    }

    public function deletePost(): void
    {
        $this->confirmDestructiveListAction(
            destroy: fn (Post $post) => $post->delete(),
            ability: 'delete',
            successMessage: 'Post deleted',
        );
    }

    public function navTitle(): string
    {
        return 'Posts';
    }

    public function render(): View
    {
        return view('native.posts');
    }

    private function posts(ListPage $page)
    {
        return Post::query()
            ->when($this->query !== '', fn ($query) => $query->where('title', 'like', '%'.$this->query.'%'))
            ->latest()
            ->paginate(perPage: 20, page: $page->page);
    }
}
```

`updatedQuery()` runs whenever PHP accepts a new query, so the list restarts
from page one for each search. Keys passed to `openPost()` and
`requestDeletion()` are model ids, never loop positions.

## 3. Write the view

Save this as `resources/views/native/posts.blade.php`:

```blade
<native:column class="w-full flex-1">
    <firstlight:search-field
        placeholder="Search posts"
        a11y-label="Search posts"
        native:model.debounce.300ms="query"
        class="mx-4 my-2"
    />

    @if (count($listItems) === 0)
        <firstlight:status-label
            label="{{ $query === '' ? 'No posts yet' : 'No matching posts' }}"
            tone="neutral"
            class="mx-4"
        />
    @endif

    <firstlight:list separator @refresh="reload" @endReached="loadMore" class="flex-1">
        @foreach ($listItems as $post)
            <firstlight:list-item
                :headline="$post->title"
                :supporting="$post->excerpt"
                trailing-icon="chevron-right"
                trailing-icon-ios="chevron.right"
                trailing-icon-android="chevron_right"
                @press="openPost({{ $post->id }})"
                :trailing-actions="[
                    ['method' => 'requestDeletion('.$post->id.')', 'label' => 'Delete', 'role' => 'destructive'],
                ]"
            />
        @endforeach
    </firstlight:list>

    <firstlight:confirmation-dialog
        :visible="$confirmingListDestruction"
        title="Delete post?"
        message="This action cannot be undone."
        confirm-label="Delete"
        cancel-label="Keep post"
        tone="destructive"
        @press="deletePost"
        @dismiss="cancelDeletion"
    />
</native:column>
```

## What each platform shows

| Behaviour | iOS | Android |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Search | `UISearchTextField` with the system clear button | Material 3 search field with the search IME action |
| Rows | SwiftUI `List` rows with dividers | `LazyColumn` Material list items with dividers |
| Refresh | System pull-to-refresh | Material pull-to-refresh |
| Delete | Trailing swipe action, then a native confirmation dialog | Trailing swipe action, then a native confirmation dialog |
| Feedback | "Post deleted" through Transient Feedback | "Post deleted" through Transient Feedback |

The same Blade works on both platforms. Swipe actions are also exposed as
VoiceOver and TalkBack actions, so screen-reader users can delete without a
swipe gesture.

## Rules to keep

- Keep `@endReached` bound even on the last page; extra events are ignored.
- Do not omit the Delete action for rows the Policy denies. Disable the row
  with `:disabled` instead, as described in [Authorize actions](authorize-actions.md).
- Full swipes never delete. The swipe only opens the confirmation dialog, and
  PHP authorizes again before deleting.
- Use `native:model.debounce.300ms` for search so each keystroke does not
  query the database.

## Adapt the recipe

- **No deletion:** remove `trailing-actions`, the dialog, and the three
  deletion methods.
- **Cursor pagination:** pass `$page->cursor` to `cursorPaginate()`, as shown
  in [Paginate lists](paginate-lists.md#cursor-pagination).
- **Search on submit instead of while typing:** bind `native:model.lazy="query"`.

--- Source: docs/how-to/build-a-form-screen.md ---

# Build a Form Screen

This recipe builds the create screen most apps need: labelled fields, Laravel
validation through a Form Request, errors shown by each native field, an error
for problems that belong to the whole form, a Save button with a loading state,
and a return to the previous screen with success Feedback.

This recipe runs unchanged in the
[showcase app](https://github.com/firstlightui/showcase), where
[`FormRecipeTest`](https://github.com/firstlightui/showcase/blob/main/tests/Feature/Recipes/FormRecipeTest.php)
exercises it.

Use it when several values are checked and saved together. Use the
[settings recipe](build-a-settings-screen.md) when each value saves on its own.

## 1. Register the route

```php
use App\NativeComponents\CreatePostScreen;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::native('/posts/create', CreatePostScreen::class)->name('posts.create');
```

Register it before any `/posts/{post}` route so `create` is not read as an id.

## 2. Write the Form Request

```php
<?php

namespace App\Http\Requests;

use Illuminate\Foundation\Http\FormRequest;

class StorePostRequest extends FormRequest
{
    public function rules(): array
    {
        return [
            'title' => 'required|min:3|max:80',
            'body' => 'required|min:10',
        ];
    }

    public function messages(): array
    {
        return [
            'body.min' => 'Write at least a sentence.',
        ];
    }
}
```

Declare rules in the order the fields appear. The error summary lists messages
in rule order.

## 3. Write the screen

```php
<?php

namespace App\NativeComponents;

use App\Http\Requests\StorePostRequest;
use App\Models\Post;
use FirstlightUI\NativeComponent;
use Illuminate\Validation\ValidationException;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class CreatePostScreen extends NativeComponent
{
    public string $title = '';

    public string $body = '';

    public function save(): void
    {
        $saved = $this->submit(
            action: function (): void {
                $this->validate(StorePostRequest::class);

                if (Post::query()->where('title', $this->title)->exists()) {
                    throw ValidationException::withMessages([
                        'form' => 'A post with this title already exists.',
                    ]);
                }

                Post::query()->create([
                    'title' => $this->title,
                    'excerpt' => str($this->body)->limit(60)->toString(),
                    'body' => $this->body,
                ]);
            },
            successMessage: 'Post created',
            validate: false,
        );

        if ($saved) {
            $this->back();
        }
    }

    public function navTitle(): string
    {
        return 'New post';
    }

    public function render(): View
    {
        return view('native.create-post');
    }
}
```

`validate: false` stops `submit()` from running `$rules` first, because the Form
Request supplies them inside the action. Any `ValidationException` thrown inside
the action, from the Form Request or from your own check, is shown on the
screen and `submit()` returns `false`.

## 4. Write the view

Save this as `resources/views/native/create-post.blade.php`:

```blade
<native:scroll-view class="w-full flex-1">
    <native:column class="w-full p-4 gap-4">
        <firstlight:callout error-for="form" />

        <firstlight:text-field
            label="Title"
            autocapitalize="sentences"
            submit-label="next"
            native:model="title"
            required
        />

        <firstlight:text-area
            label="Body"
            native:model="body"
            required
        />

        <firstlight:button variant="primary" :loading="$submitting" @press="save">
            Save post
        </firstlight:button>
    </native:column>
</native:scroll-view>
```

No `:error` wiring is needed. After a failed save, each field shows its first
message in its native error slot, and the Callout shows the `form` message.
For long forms, add `<firstlight:callout error-summary />` above the fields to
list every message in one place.

## What each platform shows

| Behaviour | iOS | Android |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Field errors | Error text under the field with error colouring | Material 3 supporting text in the error state |
| Form error | Danger Callout | Danger Callout |
| Screen reader | VoiceOver reads the errors and moves to the first invalid field | TalkBack reads the errors and moves to the first invalid field |
| Success | Returns to the previous screen and shows "Post created" | Returns to the previous screen and shows "Post created" |

## Rules to keep

- Do not wrap `save()` in `try`/`catch`. Firstlight shows validation errors for
  you.
- Do not place `@nativeError` next to Firstlight fields. It skips native error
  colouring and screen-reader announcements.
- Use a key that is not a field name, such as `form`, for errors that belong to
  the whole form.
- `required` on a field is display only. The Form Request enforces it.

## Adapt the recipe

- **Edit instead of create:** load the model in `mount()`, copy its values into
  the properties, and call `update()` instead of `create()`.
- **Validate as the user leaves a field:** add
  `public function updatedTitle(): void { $this->validateOnly('title', StorePostRequest::class); }`.
- **Test it:** see [Test screens](test-screens.md).

--- Source: docs/how-to/build-a-settings-screen.md ---

# Build a Settings Screen

This recipe builds a standard settings screen: grouped sections with headers
and footers, switches and pickers that save as soon as they change, and rows
that open other screens.

This recipe runs unchanged in the
[showcase app](https://github.com/firstlightui/showcase), where
[`SettingsRecipeTest`](https://github.com/firstlightui/showcase/blob/main/tests/Feature/Recipes/SettingsRecipeTest.php)
exercises it.

Use it for preferences the user changes one at a time. Use the
[form recipe](build-a-form-screen.md) instead when several fields must be
validated and saved together with a button.

## How the pieces fit

Settings controls are not List Item rows, so the container is Mobile UI's
`native:list` with `native:list-section`, not `firstlight:list`. Mobile UI
renders that container with a SwiftUI `List` in the inset-grouped style on iOS
and grouped Material sections on Android. There is no settings tag to learn.

Mobile UI gives each row no padding and, on iOS, no background. List Item pads
itself, but Switch and Select do not, so their labels would touch the card edge
and the first letter can be clipped. Wrap each row in a `native:column` with
`px-4 py-3 bg-theme-surface`: the padding gives the native row insets, and the
surface colour draws the grouped card on iOS and matches List Item's surface on
Android. Add `separator` to the list so iOS draws dividers between rows in a
card; Android always does.

## 1. Register the route

```php
use App\NativeComponents\SettingsScreen;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::native('/settings', SettingsScreen::class)->name('settings');
```

## 2. Write the screen

Each setting is a public property. `updated{Property}` runs when PHP accepts a
new value, so it is where the value is saved. This example stores values with
Laravel's cache; use your own model or storage instead.

```php
<?php

namespace App\NativeComponents;

use FirstlightUI\NativeComponent;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Cache;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class SettingsScreen extends NativeComponent
{
    public bool $notifications = true;

    public bool $marketing = false;

    public string $digest = 'weekly';

    /** @var array<string, string> */
    public array $digestOptions = [
        'daily' => 'Daily',
        'weekly' => 'Weekly',
        'never' => 'Never',
    ];

    public function mount(): void
    {
        $this->notifications = Cache::get('settings.notifications', true);
        $this->marketing = Cache::get('settings.marketing', false);
        $this->digest = Cache::get('settings.digest', 'weekly');
    }

    public function updatedNotifications(bool $value): void
    {
        Cache::forever('settings.notifications', $value);
    }

    public function updatedMarketing(bool $value): void
    {
        Cache::forever('settings.marketing', $value);
    }

    public function updatedDigest(string $value): void
    {
        Cache::forever('settings.digest', $value);
    }

    public function openPrivacy(): void
    {
        $this->navigate('/settings/privacy');
    }

    public function navTitle(): string
    {
        return 'Settings';
    }

    public function render(): View
    {
        return view('native.settings');
    }
}
```

## 3. Write the view

Save this as `resources/views/native/settings.blade.php`:

```blade
<native:list class="w-full flex-1" separator>
    <native:list-section header="Notifications" footer="Alerts for replies and mentions.">
        <native:column class="w-full px-4 py-3 bg-theme-surface">
            <firstlight:switch label="Push notifications" native:model="notifications" />
        </native:column>
        <native:column class="w-full px-4 py-3 bg-theme-surface">
            <firstlight:switch label="Product news" native:model="marketing" />
        </native:column>
    </native:list-section>

    <native:list-section header="Email" footer="A summary of activity you missed.">
        <native:column class="w-full px-4 py-3 bg-theme-surface">
            <firstlight:select label="Digest" :options="$digestOptions" native:model="digest" />
        </native:column>
    </native:list-section>

    <native:list-section header="Account">
        <native:column class="w-full bg-theme-surface">
            <firstlight:list-item
                headline="Privacy"
                trailing-icon="chevron-right"
                trailing-icon-ios="chevron.right"
                trailing-icon-android="chevron_right"
                @press="openPrivacy"
            />
        </native:column>
    </native:list-section>
</native:list>
```

## What each platform shows

| Behaviour | iOS | Android |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grouping | SwiftUI `List` in the inset-grouped style; the row columns paint the cards | Rounded section cards with headers and footers, drawn by Mobile UI |
| Row insets | The row column's `px-4 py-3` | The row column's `px-4 py-3` inside the card's 16 dp margin |
| Dividers | Between rows when the list sets `separator` | Always between rows in a card |
| Switches | SwiftUI `Toggle` | Material 3 `Switch` |
| Digest | Native menu picker | Material 3 exposed dropdown |
| Privacy row | List Item row with a chevron | Material list item with a chevron |

## Rules to keep

- Save in `updated{Property}`, not in a Save button. Settings screens apply each
  change immediately.
- Wrap every control row in a padded `native:column` with
  `bg-theme-surface`. Rows placed straight in a section have no insets.
- Keep a section footer short. It explains the section, not each control.
- Use `firstlight:list` only when every row is a List Item, such as a list of
  records. Settings mix controls, so they use `native:list`.
- Put the screen under a layout that uses native chrome, as described in
  [Build a list and detail flow](build-a-list-detail-flow.md), so the title and
  back navigation come from the platform.

--- Source: docs/getting-started/installation.md ---

# Install Firstlight UI

Firstlight is the app-shell layer for NativePHP. After these steps your app,
and your coding agent, can build lists and detail, search, forms with Laravel
validation, settings, sheets and dialogs, and feedback from genuine SwiftUI and
Jetpack Compose controls.

## Requirements

Start with a NativePHP Mobile 4 application that meets the [current compatibility requirements](../reference/compatibility.md).

Use NativePHP Mobile `^4.6` and Mobile UI `^0.8`. Firstlight screens must
extend `FirstlightUI\NativeComponent` for the
[response-revision contract](../reference/compatibility.md#runtime-response-contract).
Firstlight 1.0.0 is a release candidate pending physical-device,
soak/performance, and wider app qualification.

## Install and register the plugin

Install Firstlight as a normal Composer dependency. Until 1.0.0 is stable,
allow release candidates in the constraint; Laravel's default minimum
stability otherwise finds no installable version:

```bash
composer require "firstlightui/nativephp:^1.0@RC"
```

Laravel discovers `FirstlightUI\FirstlightServiceProvider` from the package metadata. Register the native plugin explicitly so NativePHP adds the renderers declared in `nativephp.json` to the application:

```bash
php artisan native:plugin:register
```

The command discovers unregistered plugins. If your application disables Laravel package discovery, register `FirstlightUI\FirstlightServiceProvider` through the application's normal provider configuration as well.

## Rebuild the native projects

Native renderer source is compiled into the host application. Regenerate the native projects after installing or updating Firstlight:

```bash
php artisan native:install --force
```

Build and run the application through your normal NativePHP workflow. Firstlight's `<firstlight:...>` tags are collected as native elements only in a native render; an ordinary web render leaves them unchanged.

## Give your coding agent the Firstlight guideline

Firstlight ships a Laravel Boost guideline and two skills. Install Boost so
your coding agent builds screens from the Firstlight recipes:

```bash
composer require laravel/boost --dev
php artisan boost:install
```

If Boost is already installed, run `php artisan boost:update --discover`
instead. See [Build with a coding agent](build-with-a-coding-agent.md) for what
the agent receives.

## Next step

Build the app shell with the
[list and detail recipe](../how-to/build-a-list-detail-flow.md), then add the
[searchable list](../how-to/build-a-searchable-list-screen.md),
[form](../how-to/build-a-form-screen.md), and
[settings](../how-to/build-a-settings-screen.md) screens your app needs. To
learn one control at a time instead, add
[your first Firstlight component](first-component.md).

--- Source: docs/getting-started/build-with-a-coding-agent.md ---

# Build with a Coding Agent

Firstlight is written to be built with by coding agents. The package ships a
[Laravel Boost](https://laravel.com/docs/boost) guideline and two Boost skills,
and its documentation is published as `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt`. Together
they tell an agent which screens to build from which recipe, which control to
use for each value, and which mistakes to avoid.

## Set up Boost

Install Firstlight as described in [Installation](installation.md), then add
Laravel Boost to the application and run its installer:

```bash
composer require laravel/boost --dev
php artisan boost:install
```

Boost finds the guideline and skills in Firstlight's `resources/boost`
directory and writes them into your agent's files, such as `AGENTS.md`,
`CLAUDE.md`, and its skills directory. If Boost is already installed, pick up
Firstlight with:

```bash
php artisan boost:update --discover
```

Run `php artisan boost:update` after each Firstlight update so the guideline
and skills match the installed version.

## What your agent gets

| Resource | When the agent reads it | What it contains |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Guideline | Always, as part of the agent's instructions | The rules every Firstlight screen follows, the four recipes, the screen generator, and a tested example |
| `firstlight-init` skill | When asked to set up or scaffold a Firstlight app | An interview, an install check, the theme, the native-chrome layout, and the chosen recipe screens with tests |
| `building-firstlight-screens` skill | When adding or changing a screen, form, list, or settings page | Which recipe to start from, which control fits each value, the workflow, and what never to do |
| [`llms.txt`](https://firstlightui.dev/llms.txt) | When the agent needs a page | Every documentation page with a one-line summary |
| [`llms-full.txt`](https://firstlightui.dev/llms-full.txt) | When the agent needs the whole reference | The full text of every documentation page in one file |

The package also includes `llms-full.txt` at
`vendor/firstlightui/nativephp/llms-full.txt`, so an agent can read the
reference for the installed version without network access.

### The guideline's rules

The guideline keeps an agent on the same path as the recipes:

- Screens extend `FirstlightUI\NativeComponent`.
- Controls are `<firstlight:*>` tags, with one Blade view for both platforms.
- Navigation chrome comes from NativePHP: layouts return `true` from
  `usesNativeChrome()`. No custom-drawn tab bars, drawers, charts, or carousels.
- Validation is Laravel validation, with `$rules` or a Form Request passed to
  `$this->validate()`. Fields show their own errors.
- Destructive actions open a Confirmation Dialog and authorize in PHP.
- Colours come from the NativePHP theme, not from markup.

## Ask for an app

With Boost installed, describe the app rather than the controls. For example:

> Set up this app with Firstlight. The main record is a job. I want a
> searchable list of jobs, a form to create one, and a settings screen.

The `firstlight-init` skill asks about the record, the recipes, brand colours,
tabs, deletion rules, and locale one question at a time, and makes no change
you have not agreed to. It then scaffolds each chosen
[recipe](../how-to/build-a-list-detail-flow.md) with a Pest test and runs the
test suite.

For later screens, ask for the outcome, such as "add a screen to edit a job".
The `building-firstlight-screens` skill picks the matching recipe, or starts
from the generator:

```bash
php artisan make:firstlight-screen EditJob --form --test
```

## What still needs a person

An agent can write screens and run their Pest tests. It cannot see the app on
a device. Both skills end by asking you to run the app on an iOS simulator and
an Android emulator and check navigation, field errors, and deletion on both.
Check accessibility too. See [Accessibility](../concepts/accessibility.md) for
what Firstlight covers and what your app still owns.

--- Source: docs/getting-started/first-component.md ---

# Add Your First Firstlight Component

This tutorial adds a native Segmented control for choosing a queue. The same EDGE markup renders as a platform-appropriate control on iOS and Android.

## Define the state

Extend Firstlight's base for your screen, rather than the upstream EDGE base:

```php
use FirstlightUI\NativeComponent;

class QueueScreen extends NativeComponent
{
    // Add the state below; use your normal Blade view.
}
```

Normal Blade renders (a global `View` returned from `render()`, `$this->view()`,
or an inferred view) automatically receive normal chrome and a root response
revision. For a hand-built Element root, return `$this->response($element)`
from `render()` instead of returning the Element directly. Nested children are
untouched and partials are unstamped. Streaming is disabled and cannot be opted
into. See the [full contract and limits](../reference/compatibility.md#runtime-response-contract).

Add the selected value and stable value-to-label options to your component:

```php
public string $queue = 'mine';

public array $queueOptions = [
    'mine' => 'Mine',
    'all' => 'All',
];
```

The array keys are the public values stored in `$queue`; the labels are display text.

## Render the control

Bind the property with `native:model`:

```blade
<firstlight:segmented
    :options="$queueOptions"
    native:model="queue"
    label="Queue"
    helper="Choose the active queue."
/>
```

Run the application natively. A selection emits its stable value to PHP, and the published `$queue` value determines the visible selection.

## Handle a selection explicitly

Use `@change` when the selection should call a method instead of directly synchronising a property:

```blade
<firstlight:segmented
    :options="$queueOptions"
    :value="$queue"
    @change="selectQueue"
    label="Queue"
/>
```

The method receives the selected string value. See the [Segmented reference](../components/segmented.md) for integer values, disabled choices, accessibility, and validation rules. When the screen should show Laravel messages on Firstlight fields, follow [Validate fields](../how-to/validate-fields.md).

--- Source: docs/getting-started/theming.md ---

# Theme Firstlight Components

Firstlight components inherit the semantic theme from `nativephp/mobile-ui`. There is no separate Firstlight theme file: configure the host application once, and the same tokens reach the native SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose renderers.

The theme changes colour and typography while each platform retains its native geometry, motion, and interaction.

## Publish the theme configuration

Publish `config/native-ui.php` into the application:

```shell
php artisan vendor:publish --tag=native-ui-config
```

## Set the brand colour pairs

Set both the background token and its `on-*` content token. This example uses the Firstlight showcase palette; replace the values with accessible pairs from your own brand:

```php
'theme' => [
    'light' => [
        'primary' => '#AE1515',
        'on-primary' => '#FFF5EA',
    ],
    'dark' => [
        'primary' => '#ED4E0C',
        'on-primary' => '#110805',
    ],
],
```

The `primary` pair colours filled actions, selected states, and key accents. Surface, outline, destructive, success, accent, and disabled-state colours use their corresponding semantic tokens from the published configuration.

Dark values are optional because NativePHP can derive them from the light theme. Define explicit dark overrides when brand perception or contrast needs a tuned pair. Keep text and icons at a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against their background token.

Theme colours accept CSS hex values, Tailwind palette names such as `violet-600`, and opacity modifiers such as `violet-600/15`.

## Set warning colours

Status Label, Badge, Callout, and Transient Feedback share the `warning` / `on-warning` pair on both platforms, independently of the brand `accent` pair. Add these keys to the same theme blocks:

```php
'light' => ['warning' => '#B45309', 'on-warning' => '#FFFFFF'],
'dark' => ['warning' => '#FBBF24', 'on-warning' => '#1C1917'],
```

These are also the fallback pairs when the effective theme has no corresponding warning token. NativePHP can derive dark values from configured light values; explicit dark overrides keep the intended amber presentation. All four surfaces share contrast-safe black/white text correction for inaccessible authored pairs. List Item's `leading-icon-tone="warning"` and `trailing-icon-tone="warning"` use the same warning colour in the active appearance.

Firstlight resolves these open-ended theme keys in PHP and publishes them with each component tree, because the native theme token structs do not retain custom keys. After a runtime `Theme::merge()`, republish the component tree to update warning colours. The light/dark pair already in that tree switches immediately with the native appearance.

## Use theme tokens in surrounding native UI

Firstlight controls consume the tokens automatically. Use the same tokens for surrounding `nativephp/mobile-ui` elements with theme-aware utility classes:

```blade
<native:column class="bg-theme-surface border border-theme-outline rounded-2xl p-4">
    <native:text class="text-theme-on-surface text-lg font-bold">
        Account
    </native:text>

    <firstlight:text-field
        label="Email"
        native:model="email"
    />
</native:column>
```

## Apply a runtime brand

For tenant or user-specific branding, merge only the tokens that change from a service provider:

```php
use Native\Mobile\UI\Theme;

public function boot(): void
{
    Theme::merge([
        'light' => [
            'primary' => '#AE1515',
            'on-primary' => '#FFF5EA',
        ],
        'dark' => [
            'primary' => '#ED4E0C',
            'on-primary' => '#110805',
        ],
    ]);
}
```

`Theme::merge()` deep-merges the new values, synchronises the effective Laravel configuration, and publishes the updated tokens to the native renderers.

--- Source: docs/how-to/validate-fields.md ---

# Validate Firstlight Fields

NativePHP EDGE has no built-in `validate()`. Firstlight adds a Livewire-shaped
Laravel Validator layer. A screen that opts in can call `$this->validate()` or
`$this->validateOnly()`, and participating fields show the first `MessageBag`
message in the native `error` slot.

Do not place `@nativeError` next to Firstlight fields. That directive emits a
sibling text node and skips native field error colour, helper replacement, and
accessibility. Use `ValidatesFields`, `error-for`, or an authored `error`
instead.

The method contract, participating fields, and current limitations are listed
in the [ValidatesFields reference](../reference/validates-fields.md).

## Opt in

Extend `FirstlightUI\NativeComponent`, which includes `ValidatesFields` and
the full nonstreaming response-revision contract:

```php
use FirstlightUI\NativeComponent;

class SignupScreen extends NativeComponent
{
}
```

The trait remains usable separately, but adding it to the upstream EDGE base
does not provide the publication contract. Blade render paths are automatic;
programmatic Element roots must return `$this->response($element)` to add normal
chrome and the revision. Nested children are untouched, partials are unstamped,
and streaming cannot be opted into. Repeated validation responses use this
same contract, not a per-event acknowledgement. See
[Compatibility](../reference/compatibility.md#runtime-response-contract).

## Declare rules and bind fields

Rule keys must match public property names (`email` ↔ `native:model="email"`).
Nested and wildcard keys are not supported.

```php
public string $name = '';

public string $email = '';

public bool $accepted = false;

/** @var array<string, string> */
protected array $rules = [
    'name' => 'required|min:2',
    'email' => 'required|email',
    'accepted' => 'accepted',
];

/** @var array<string, string> */
protected array $validationAttributes = [
    'accepted' => 'terms',
];

public function updatedEmail(): void
{
    $this->validateOnly('email');
}

public function save(): void
{
    $this->validate();
}
```

```blade
<firstlight:text-field label="Name" native:model.blur="name" />
<firstlight:text-field
    label="Email"
    keyboard="email"
    content-type="email"
    autocapitalize="none"
    :autocorrect="false"
    native:model.blur="email"
/>
<firstlight:checkbox label="I agree to the terms" native:model="accepted" />
<firstlight:button label="Continue" @press="save" />
```

No `:error` wiring is required. After a failed `validate()` or
`validateOnly()`, the next published frame fills each field's `error` from
`MessageBag::first($field)`. `required` on a field is display metadata only;
Laravel `required`, `accepted`, and other rules remain the enforcement.

You do not wrap `@press` handlers in `try`/`catch`. Firstlight stores the
exception's bag and republishes the screen with field messages.

## Validate one field on blur or live

`updated{Property}` runs when PHP accepts that property. Pair it with the sync
mode that should trigger the check.

Blur publishes on focus loss, then validates only that key:

```blade
<firstlight:text-field label="Email" native:model.blur="email" />
```

```php
public function updatedEmail(): void
{
    $this->validateOnly('email');
}
```

Live publishes while editing:

```blade
<firstlight:text-field label="Email" native:model.live="email" />
```

`validateOnly('email')` replaces only the `email` messages. Other keys already
in the bag stay put. A passing `validateOnly()` clears that key.

You can call `validateOnly()` from `@change` or `@submit` instead of
`updated{Property}` when the field should invoke a named method.

## Use a Form Request

Pass a class name to `validate()` or `validateOnly()`. Firstlight reads that
object's `rules()`, `messages()`, and `attributes()` and runs them against the
screen's public properties. It does not perform an HTTP redirect.

```php
use Illuminate\Foundation\Http\FormRequest;

class StoreSignupRequest extends FormRequest
{
    public function rules(): array
    {
        return [
            'name' => 'required|min:2',
            'email' => 'required|email',
            'accepted' => 'accepted',
        ];
    }

    public function messages(): array
    {
        return [
            'email.required' => 'Need an email address.',
        ];
    }

    public function attributes(): array
    {
        return [
            'accepted' => 'terms',
        ];
    }
}
```

```php
public function save(): void
{
    $this->validate(StoreSignupRequest::class);
}
```

`authorize()` and other Form Request HTTP behaviour are unused. You can also
pass a plain class that implements those three methods.

## Bind a different MessageBag key

When the rule key differs from the model name, set `error-for`:

```blade
<firstlight:text-field
    label="Work email"
    native:model="email"
    error-for="contact_email"
/>
```

```php
protected array $rules = [
    'contact_email' => 'required|email',
];
```

`error-for` wins over `native:model` when both are present.

## Let an authored error win

A non-empty authored `error` attribute wins over the MessageBag. Use it for
application-specific copy that should not come from Laravel rules:

```blade
<firstlight:text-field
    label="Email"
    native:model="email"
    error="This account is already registered."
/>
```

An empty authored `error` is treated as unset, so the bag can still fill the
slot. You can also bind explicitly from the `$errorBag` the trait shares with
the view:

```blade
<firstlight:text-field
    label="Email"
    native:model.blur="email"
    :error="$errorBag->first('email')"
/>
```

## Add and clear messages

Use the same bag for server-side checks that are not Laravel rules:

```php
public function save(): void
{
    $this->validate();

    if ($this->emailIsTaken()) {
        $this->addError('email', 'This account is already registered.');

        return;
    }

    $this->resetValidation();
}
```

`resetValidation('email')` forgets one key. `resetValidation()` clears the
bag. `hasError('email')` and `getErrorBag()` inspect the current messages.

## Show form-level errors

Some failures belong to the form, not one field: wrong credentials, a declined
card, a server conflict. Add them under a key no field uses and show that key
with a Callout:

```php
public function signIn(): void
{
    $this->validate();

    if (! Auth::attempt(['email' => $this->email, 'password' => $this->password])) {
        $this->addError('form', 'These credentials do not match our records.');
    }
}
```

```blade
<firstlight:callout error-for="form" />
<firstlight:text-field label="Email" native:model.blur="email" />
<firstlight:text-field label="Password" secure native:model.blur="password" />
<firstlight:button label="Sign in" @press="signIn" />
```

To summarise every message above a long form, use `error-summary`:

```blade
<firstlight:callout error-summary />
```

The summary lists each key's first message in bag order, which follows your
rules, so declare rules in the order the fields appear. One message is shown
alone; two or more get a heading such as `There are 3 errors.` and one message
per line.

Both Callouts default to the `danger` tone, take their text from the bag (so
`message` is rejected), and render nothing while there is nothing to show. You
can still set `tone` or add an `action-label` with `@press`. `error-for` and
`error-summary` cannot be combined.

## Screen-reader announcements

After a failed interaction, Firstlight announces the errors once:

- **A press or keyboard submit** (Button `@press`, field `@submit`) speaks the
  whole summary, for example `There are 2 errors. The name field is required.
  The email field is required.`, and moves screen-reader focus to the first
  invalid field on the screen.
- **A field update** (`native:model.blur`, `.live`, `@change`, and
  `updated{Property}` hooks) speaks only the message that update just added
  and leaves focus where it is.

On iOS, VoiceOver focus moves to the first invalid field and the announcement
follows it; the keyboard does not open. On Android, while TalkBack is on, Text
Field, Text Area, and Code Editor take input focus, which TalkBack follows and
reads with the error, and the keyboard opens; other fields only announce,
because Android moves focus only to editable text. Nothing is spoken when no message was added, and republishing
the same screen does not repeat the announcement.

The summary heading is package chrome. Translate it by publishing the language
files (see [Localize chrome](localize.md)) and editing
`lang/vendor/firstlight/{locale}/validation.php`.

The `/captures/form-errors` showcase route shows a summary above failed
fields:

| Platform | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- |
| iOS | ![Form error summary on iOS in light mode](../screenshots/form-errors/ios-light.png) | ![Form error summary on iOS in dark mode](../screenshots/form-errors/ios-dark.png) |
| Android | ![Form error summary on Android in light mode](../screenshots/form-errors/android-light.png) | ![Form error summary on Android in dark mode](../screenshots/form-errors/android-dark.png) |

## Do not validate during mount or render

`mount()` and `render()` still sit on NativePHP's generic `Throwable` overlay
path. Throwing `ValidationException` there paints the red error overlay instead
of field messages. Call `validate()` and `validateOnly()` from actions,
`@submit` / `@change` handlers, and `updated{Property}` hooks.

`addError()` does not throw and is safe from `render()` when a fixture needs a
stable failed frame.

## Screenshots

These development screenshots were captured from the dedicated
`/captures/validate-fields` showcase route. The interactive dogfood screen is
`/validation`.

| Platform | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- |
| iOS | ![Failed Laravel field validation on iOS in light mode](../screenshots/validate-fields/ios-light.png) | ![Failed Laravel field validation on iOS in dark mode](../screenshots/validate-fields/ios-dark.png) |
| Android | ![Failed Laravel field validation on Android in light mode](../screenshots/validate-fields/android-light.png) | ![Failed Laravel field validation on Android in dark mode](../screenshots/validate-fields/android-dark.png) |

--- Source: docs/how-to/submit-forms.md ---

# Submit Firstlight Forms

Firstlight submits forms through an ordinary Button press and a PHP screen
method. There is no `<firstlight:form>` container, client-side validator, or
form schema.

## Declare the screen

Extend `FirstlightUI\NativeComponent` to use the form submission and field
validation helpers. Declare Laravel rules against the public properties bound
by your fields:

```php
<?php

namespace App\Native;

use App\Models\Profile;
use FirstlightUI\NativeComponent;

class EditProfileScreen extends NativeComponent
{
    public string $name = '';

    public string $email = '';

    protected array $rules = [
        'name' => 'required',
        'email' => 'required|email',
    ];

    public function save(): void
    {
        $this->submit(
            action: fn () => Profile::query()->updateOrCreate(
                ['user_id' => auth()->id()],
                ['name' => $this->name, 'email' => $this->email],
            ),
            successMessage: 'Profile saved',
        );
    }
}
```

Screens that extend `Native\Mobile\Edge\NativeComponent` directly can opt in
with both `FirstlightUI\Concerns\ValidatesFields` and
`FirstlightUI\Concerns\SubmitsForms`.

## Bind the fields and Button

Use the existing fields, `native:model`, and Button:

```blade
<firstlight:text-field
    label="Name"
    native:model.blur="name"
/>

<firstlight:text-field
    label="Email"
    native:model.blur="email"
/>

<firstlight:button @press="save">
    Save profile
</firstlight:button>
```

`submit()` runs `$this->validate()` first. A validation failure returns
`false`, skips the callable and success Feedback, and lets
`ValidatesFields` publish each first Laravel message through the matching
field's native `error` slot. Screen readers hear a summary and move to the
first invalid field; add `<firstlight:callout error-summary />` for a visible
summary. See [Validate Firstlight fields](validate-fields.md)
for rule sources, Form Requests, custom messages, and explicit error binding. The
[ValidatesFields reference](../reference/validates-fields.md) lists the method
contract and participating fields.

After successful validation, `submit()` runs the callable and sends
`Feedback::success($successMessage)->send()` when the message is non-empty.
It then returns `true`. Pass `validate: false` only when the action does not
need field validation:

```php
$sent = $this->submit(
    action: fn () => $this->sendVerificationEmail(),
    successMessage: 'Verification email sent',
    validate: false,
);
```

To fail the whole form from inside the action, throw Laravel's
`ValidationException`. Its messages replace the screen's error bag, `submit()`
returns `false`, and no success Feedback is sent:

```php
use Illuminate\Validation\ValidationException;

$this->submit(
    action: function (): void {
        if (! Auth::attempt(['email' => $this->email, 'password' => $this->password])) {
            throw ValidationException::withMessages([
                'form' => 'These credentials do not match our records.',
            ]);
        }
    },
    successMessage: 'Signed in',
);
```

```blade
<firstlight:callout error-for="form" />
```

Other unexpected exceptions from the callable are not converted to Feedback or
swallowed.

## Loading and duplicate submissions

`$submitting` is `true` while validation and the callable run. Re-entering
`submit()` on the same PHP component during that interval returns `false`
without validating, calling the action, or sending Feedback. `submit()` always
clears `$submitting` in `finally`, so binding Button `loading` or `disabled` to
`$this->submitting` does not flash during the default one-request path.

NativePHP handles a press and then compiles one Element Tree afterward. A
device-visible loading frame requires application code to set `$this->submitting
= true` outside `submit()`, publish that tree, and clear the flag on a later
request.

The helper does not publish an intermediate tree, call `publishPlaceholder()`,
or add a client-side loading mechanism. `publishPlaceholder()` belongs to
lazy screen mounting, not form submission.

--- Source: docs/how-to/authorize-actions.md ---

# Authorize Firstlight Actions

Extend `FirstlightUI\NativeComponent` (or `use AuthorizesActions`) so a screen
can evaluate the current Laravel Gate or Policy before publishing or performing
an action:

```php
use App\Models\Post;
use FirstlightUI\NativeComponent;

class PostScreen extends NativeComponent
{
    public Post $post;
    public bool $confirmingDeletion = false;

    public function updatePost(): void
    {
        if (! $this->authorize('update', $this->post)) {
            return;
        }

        $this->post->save();
    }
}
```

`allows()` and `denies()` return booleans. `authorize()` also returns a
boolean; unlike Laravel's throwing Gate method, a denial publishes danger
Feedback with `This action is unauthorized.` and returns `false`. Keep the
guard at the start of every PHP action, even when the published control is
already hidden or disabled, because authorization can change after a frame is
published.

## Choose hide or disable

Hide an ordinary action when its absence is unsurprising:

```blade
@if ($this->allows('edit', $post))
    <firstlight:button @press="editPost">
        Edit post
    </firstlight:button>
@endif
```

Disable an action when preserving its location helps explain the available
workflow:

```blade
<firstlight:list-item
    headline="Publishing settings"
    supporting="Only editors can change publication access"
    :disabled="$this->denies('update', $post)"
    @press="openPublishingSettings"
/>
```

Button, Icon Button, and List Item all accept the existing `disabled` prop.
Firstlight does not add a `can` attribute or evaluate authorization in a
native renderer.

## Keep destructive actions visible

Never silently omit a destructive action. Keep the Button, Icon Button, or
List Item visible and disable it when denied. Supporting copy should explain
why the action is unavailable when the surrounding interface does not make
that clear.

```blade
<firstlight:button
    variant="destructive"
    :disabled="$this->denies('delete', $post)"
    @press="requestDeletion"
>
    Delete post
</firstlight:button>
```

Confirmation Dialog has no `disabled` or `loading` prop. Authorize before
setting its `visible` state, and authorize again when confirmation arrives:

```php
public function requestDeletion(): void
{
    if (! $this->authorize('delete', $this->post)) {
        $this->confirmingDeletion = false;

        return;
    }

    $this->confirmingDeletion = true;
}

public function deletePost(): void
{
    $this->confirmingDeletion = false;

    if (! $this->authorize('delete', $this->post)) {
        return;
    }

    $this->post->delete();
}

public function cancelDeletion(): void
{
    $this->confirmingDeletion = false;
}
```

```blade
<firstlight:confirmation-dialog
    :visible="$confirmingDeletion"
    title="Delete post?"
    message="This action cannot be undone."
    confirm-label="Delete"
    cancel-label="Keep post"
    tone="destructive"
    @press="deletePost"
    @dismiss="cancelDeletion"
/>
```

The denied request does not open the dialog, and `authorize()` supplies danger
Feedback instead of allowing an uncaught `AuthorizationException` to reach
NativePHP's error overlay.

For deleting rows from an accumulated `$listItems` collection by stable key,
use [Destroy list items](destroy-list-items.md).

--- Source: docs/how-to/paginate-lists.md ---

# Paginate Firstlight Lists

Firstlight paginates lists in PHP. List already exposes `@refresh` and
`@endReached`. The helper accumulates Laravel paginator pages into
`$this->listItems` so Blade can render ordinary List Item rows.

There is no `<firstlight:empty>` tag and no second scroll-event API.

## Declare the screen

Extend `FirstlightUI\NativeComponent` (or `use PaginatesLists`):

```php
<?php

namespace App\Native;

use App\Models\Conversation;
use FirstlightUI\NativeComponent;
use FirstlightUI\Pagination\ListPage;

class InboxScreen extends NativeComponent
{
    public function mount(): void
    {
        $this->reload();
    }

    public function reload(): void
    {
        $this->refreshList(
            fn (ListPage $page) => Conversation::query()->latest()->paginate(
                perPage: 20,
                page: $page->page,
            ),
        );
    }

    public function loadMore(): void
    {
        $this->loadMoreList(
            fn (ListPage $page) => Conversation::query()->latest()->paginate(
                perPage: 20,
                page: $page->page,
            ),
        );
    }
}
```

`refreshList()` replaces `$this->listItems` with the first page.
`loadMoreList()` appends the next page. Both return `false` when a fetch is
already running. `loadMoreList()` also returns `false` without querying when
`$this->listHasMore` is `false`.

Pass the paginator's `page` from `ListPage`. NativePHP has no HTTP `?page=`
query string for these events.

## Render the rows

```blade
@if (count($this->listItems) === 0)
    <firstlight:status-label
        label="No conversations yet"
        tone="neutral"
    />
    <firstlight:callout
        message="Pull to refresh after you add a conversation."
        tone="info"
    />
@endif

<firstlight:list separator @refresh="reload" @endReached="loadMore">
    @foreach ($this->listItems as $conversation)
        <firstlight:list-item
            :headline="$conversation->title"
            @press="openConversation"
        />
    @endforeach
</firstlight:list>
```

Keep `@endReached` bound even on the last page. Extra events are ignored.

Empty copy is ordinary Blade around List. Compose Status Label, Callout, and
Button when you need a retry action.

## Cursor pagination

`ListPage::$cursor` is `null` on refresh and the previous paginator's next
cursor afterward. Pass it through to `cursorPaginate()`:

```php
use Illuminate\Pagination\Cursor;

$this->refreshList(
    fn (ListPage $page) => Conversation::query()->latest()->cursorPaginate(
        perPage: 20,
        cursor: $page->cursor !== null ? Cursor::fromEncoded($page->cursor) : null,
    ),
);
```

Use the same callable with `loadMoreList()`.

Unexpected exceptions from the query are not converted to Feedback. Screens
that extend NativePHP's component directly can opt in with
`FirstlightUI\Concerns\PaginatesLists`.

To delete a row after Confirmation Dialog authorization, see
[Destroy list items](destroy-list-items.md).

--- Source: docs/how-to/destroy-list-items.md ---

# Destroy Firstlight List Items

Firstlight deletes list rows in PHP. Pass a stable domain key into the helper,
confirm with Confirmation Dialog, authorize again, destroy the model, and let
`$listItems` republish without that row.

An optional labelled [List Item swipe action](../components/list-item.md#swipe-actions)
can invoke the same request helper. There is no automatic swipe deletion or
renderer index. See [Authorize actions](authorize-actions.md) for
hide-versus-disable rules and [Paginate lists](paginate-lists.md) for `$listItems`.

## Declare the screen

Extend `FirstlightUI\NativeComponent` (or use `AuthorizesActions`,
`DestroysListItems`, and a `$listItems` array):

```php
<?php

namespace App\Native;

use App\Models\Post;
use FirstlightUI\NativeComponent;

class PostsScreen extends NativeComponent
{
    public function requestDeletion(int $id): void
    {
        $this->requestDestructiveListAction($id, 'delete');
    }

    public function cancelDeletion(): void
    {
        $this->cancelDestructiveListAction();
    }

    public function deletePost(): void
    {
        $this->confirmDestructiveListAction(
            destroy: fn (Post $post) => $post->delete(),
            ability: 'delete',
            successMessage: 'Post deleted',
        );
    }
}
```

`requestDestructiveListAction()` resolves the row by key from `$listItems`,
calls `authorize()`, and sets `$confirmingListDestruction` when allowed.
`confirmDestructiveListAction()` closes the dialog, authorizes again, runs the
destroy callable, removes the row from `$listItems`, and optionally sends
success Feedback.

Keys must be stable identities such as model ids. Do not pass loop indexes.

## Keep denied rows visible

```blade
<firstlight:list separator>
    @foreach ($this->listItems as $post)
        <firstlight:list-item
            :headline="$post->title"
            supporting="Delete permanently"
            :disabled="$this->denies('delete', $post)"
            @press="requestDeletion({{ $post->id }})"
        />
    @endforeach
</firstlight:list>

<firstlight:confirmation-dialog
    :visible="$confirmingListDestruction"
    title="Delete post?"
    message="This action cannot be undone."
    confirm-label="Delete"
    cancel-label="Keep post"
    tone="destructive"
    @press="deletePost"
    @dismiss="cancelDeletion"
/>
```

Never omit a destructive List Item when the Policy denies it. Disable the row
and keep supporting copy that explains the unavailable action when the
surrounding interface does not already make that clear.

To offer deletion from a swipe, add the following binding to the List Item
above. It opens the same confirmation dialog and does not remove the row:

```blade
:trailing-actions="[
    ['method' => 'requestDeletion('.$post->id.')', 'label' => 'Delete', 'role' => 'destructive'],
]"
```

Swipe callbacks use stable keys just like `@press`. A disabled row exposes no
swipe actions; authorization still runs in PHP when the action is requested and
again when deletion is confirmed.

## Custom keys or database resolve

Override `destructiveListItemKey()` when rows do not expose `getKey()`, `id`,
or an `id` array key. Override `resolveDestructiveListItem()` to reload the
model from the database instead of trusting the in-memory `$listItems` copy:

```php
protected function resolveDestructiveListItem(mixed $key): mixed
{
    return Post::query()->find($key);
}
```

When you resolve from the database, `$listItems` is still updated after a
successful destroy so the published List matches the mutation.

--- Source: docs/how-to/test-screens.md ---

# Test Firstlight Screens

Firstlight screens are tested with NativePHP's screen test harness,
`Native\Mobile\Testing\Native::test()`. The harness mounts the screen,
renders the Element Tree, and sends taps and input through the same callbacks a
device uses. Firstlight adds checks for its own controls: field errors,
List rows, Confirmation Dialog, and Feedback.

## Scaffold a screen

```bash
php artisan make:firstlight-screen Posts --form --destroy --test
```

This creates the following files:

- `app/NativeComponents/Posts.php`: a `FirstlightUI\NativeComponent` with a
  validated `name` field and `save()` (`--form`), and paginated
  `reload()`, `loadMore()`, and `listQuery()` (`--list`). It also has
  `requestDeletion()`, `cancelDeletion()`, and `deleteItem()` (`--destroy`,
  which turns on `--list`).
- `resources/views/native/posts.blade.php`: the matching Text Field, Button,
  List, and Confirmation Dialog markup.
- `tests/Feature/NativeComponents/PostsTest.php`: a Pest test that uses the
  checks below (`--test`).

Nested names such as `Settings/Notifications` create
`App\NativeComponents\Settings\Notifications` and the view
`native.settings.notifications`. The command does not overwrite existing files
unless you pass `--force`. Register the route it prints in `routes/mobile.php`.

Replace the body of `listQuery()` with your paginator query, for example
`Post::query()->latest()->paginate(perPage: 20, page: $page->page)`.

## Register the checks

Register the Firstlight checks once from `tests/Pest.php`:

```php
FirstlightUI\Testing\ScreenAssertions::register();
```

Calling it again has no effect. The generated test also calls it in
`beforeEach()`.

## Test a form

```php
use App\NativeComponents\EditProfile;
use FirstlightUI\Facades\Feedback;
use FirstlightUI\Feedback\FeedbackTone;
use Native\Mobile\Testing\Native;

it('validates and saves the profile', function () {
    Feedback::fake();

    Native::test(EditProfile::class)
        ->input('email', 'not-an-email')
        ->tap('Save')
        ->assertFieldError('email', 'The email must be a valid email address.')
        ->assertNoFeedbackSent()
        ->input('email', 'ada@example.com')
        ->tap('Save')
        ->assertNoFieldError('email')
        ->assertHasNoErrors()
        ->assertFeedbackSent('Profile saved', FeedbackTone::Success);
});
```

`assertFieldError()` reads the `error` value the field shows in the rendered
tree, so it confirms the message reached the control, not only the
MessageBag. Use `assertHasErrors()` to check the bag directly.

Select a Select, Segmented, Pill Group, or Choice Group option by its stable
value, never by its label or position:

```php
Native::test(EditProfile::class)
    ->choose('plan', 'team')
    ->assertSet('plan', 'team');
```

## Test a list and its destructive action

```php
it('deletes a post after confirmation', function () {
    Feedback::fake();

    Native::test(PostsScreen::class)
        ->assertListItem('Draft', fn (array $row) => $row['props']['disabled'] === false)
        ->pressListItem('Draft', 'Delete')
        ->assertConfirmationDialog('Delete post?')
        ->confirmDialog()
        ->assertMissingListItem('Draft')
        ->assertFeedbackSent('Post deleted');
});
```

`pressListItem('Draft')` presses the row. Pass a swipe action label as the
second argument to press that action. Both fail when the row is disabled, as
the device would ignore the press. `cancelDialog()` sends the dismissal that
both platforms send for Cancel and system dismissal.

See [Screen assertions](../reference/screen-assertions.md) for every method.

--- Source: docs/how-to/localize.md ---

# Localize Firstlight Chrome

Firstlight-owned chrome (Confirm, Cancel, OK, dismiss, clear, skip, Done,
crop, zoom, media source chooser, and password reveal) comes from one Laravel
language file. Authored labels on Confirmation Dialog and Alert Dialog still
win. Date Picker and Time Picker keep rejecting Blade `confirm-label` and
`cancel-label`; their sheet buttons are package chrome only.

The package ships English. There is no translation UI. Applications add other
locales through Laravel vendor language publishing.

## Publish the language files

```bash
php artisan vendor:publish --tag=firstlight-lang
```

Laravel copies the files to `lang/vendor/firstlight`. `validation.php` holds
the pluralised error summary heading (`'summary' => 'There is :count
error.|There are :count errors.'`) used by `error-summary` Callouts and
screen-reader announcements. Add a locale next to
English, for example `lang/vendor/firstlight/fr/chrome.php`, and keep the same
keys:

```php
<?php

return [
    'confirm' => 'Confirmer',
    'cancel' => 'Annuler',
    'ok' => 'OK',
    'dismiss' => 'Fermer',
    'dismiss_feedback' => 'Fermer le message',
    'clear' => 'Effacer',
    'clear_search' => 'Effacer la recherche',
    'clear_text' => 'Effacer le texte',
    'skip' => 'Ignorer',
    'done' => 'OK',
    'crop' => 'Recadrer',
    'zoom_in' => 'Zoom avant',
    'zoom_out' => 'Zoom arrière',
    'choose_media' => 'Choisir un média',
    'photo_library' => 'Photothèque',
    'camera' => 'Appareil photo',
    'browse_files' => 'Parcourir les fichiers',
    'show_password' => 'Afficher le mot de passe',
    'hide_password' => 'Masquer le mot de passe',
];
```

Missing keys fall back to the packaged English strings.

## Date and Time picker locale and timezone

When `locale` or `timezone` is omitted, Date Picker and Time Picker inherit
the application:

- locale from the translator (`en_AU` and `en_AU.UTF-8` become `en-AU`)
- timezone from `config('app.timezone')` when it is a real IANA identifier

Explicit picker props still win. Invalid inherited values are omitted so the
device calendar and clock are used; they do not throw. Authored malformed
`locale` or `timezone` attributes still fail before publication.

Authored field labels, helpers, errors, dialog titles, and Feedback messages
are ordinary Blade strings; translate those with `__()` as you already would.

--- Source: docs/concepts/firstlight-and-mobile-ui.md ---

# What Firstlight Is

Firstlight is the app-shell layer for NativePHP. It covers what a standard
forms app needs (lists and detail, search, forms with Laravel validation,
settings, sheets and dialogs, and feedback) with genuine SwiftUI controls on
iOS and Jetpack Compose Material 3 controls on Android, from one Blade API.

It is built for agentic coding. Four [recipes](../how-to/build-a-list-detail-flow.md)
show each kind of screen end to end, and a Laravel Boost guideline and two
skills point coding agents at them. See
[Build with a coding agent](../getting-started/build-with-a-coding-agent.md).

## Who provides what

Firstlight builds on two NativePHP packages and replaces neither.

| Layer | Provides |
| --- | --- |
| NativePHP Mobile | EDGE, the Element Tree, the event lifecycle, and native navigation chrome: layouts that return `true` from `usesNativeChrome()` get SwiftUI `NavigationStack` and `TabView` on iOS and a Material 3 `Scaffold` and top app bar on Android |
| NativePHP Mobile UI | Layout primitives such as columns, scroll views, and grouped lists, the semantic theme, and the native renderer foundation |
| Firstlight UI | Form, list, selection, overlay, status, and feedback controls with one contract on both platforms; Laravel validation, submission, authorization, pagination, and deletion on screens; Pest screen assertions and a screen generator; recipes, a Boost guideline, skills, and `llms.txt` |

Firstlight depends on Mobile UI, follows its EDGE conventions, inherits its
theme, and uses the same Element Tree and event lifecycle. Mobile UI is the
broad native toolkit; Firstlight decides common form and list behaviour once so
each application does not assemble it again.

## One API, the right pattern on each platform

A Firstlight tag means the same thing on both platforms, and each platform
draws it its own way. Tabs are a segmented control on iOS and Material 3 tabs
on Android. A Confirmation Dialog is a SwiftUI `confirmationDialog` on iOS
and a Material 3 `AlertDialog` on Android. Date Picker opens the graphical
SwiftUI `DatePicker` on iOS and the Material 3 `DatePickerDialog` on Android.
Field errors
appear under the field on iOS and as Material 3 supporting text in the error
state on Android.

Every control is a real platform control. Firstlight draws nothing to imitate
one, and there is no WebView.

## What Firstlight is not

- **Not navigation chrome.** Stacks, title bars, back navigation, and tab bars
  come from NativePHP's native chrome. Firstlight runs inside them. Do not use
  the `custom` attribute on top bars or bottom navs to draw your own.
- **Not a design system.** Firstlight does not define a visual style.
  Controls take colours and fonts from the NativePHP theme and keep each
  platform's geometry, motion, and materials.
- **Not a catalogue of everything.** There are no charts, carousels, or other
  custom-drawn controls. A new tag is added only for a semantic control with an
  equal native contract on iOS and Android.
- **Not a form builder.** Screens are ordinary Blade views with PHP state, not
  schemas.

## Additional dedicated components

Mobile UI provides primitives from which many interfaces can be composed. Firstlight adds dedicated components where one reusable semantic contract is valuable:

- **Icon Button** uses the compact native icon-button family, requires an accessible action name, guarantees minimum interaction targets, and supports disabled and loading states. Mobile UI provides capable Button and Icon primitives, but does not expose this complete contract as a standalone manifest component.
- **Search Field** makes native search behaviour an invariant. It owns the platform search and clear affordances, submit flushing, focused query state, and accessible clear action instead of requiring an application to configure a general text input each time.
- **Stepper** provides exact bounded increment and decrement over integer or floating-point grids. It uses SwiftUI `Stepper` on iOS and an idiomatic Material 3 decrement/value/increment composition on Android.
- **Status Label** provides a display-only status capsule with semantic tones, accessible static-text semantics, text scaling, and contrast protection. It avoids giving non-interactive status metadata the behaviour of a button or selectable chip.

## Higher-level components over existing primitives

Some Firstlight components package several Mobile UI capabilities into one stable application-facing value:

- **Choice Group** presents single-choice radio rows or multiple-choice checkbox rows through one option-array API and one complete scalar-or-list value.
- **Pill Group** composes native chip intents into one single- or multiple-selection field. The group publishes one stable scalar or list rather than requiring a separate Boolean model for every chip.
- **Text Area** turns multiline editing into a dedicated, deliberately narrow field with native focused-state preservation, line bounds, validation feedback, and a genuine SwiftUI `TextEditor` expression on iOS.
- **Time Picker** separates nullable `HH:mm` selection from a combined date/time/datetime API and gives it the same explicit draft, confirmation, validation, and accepted-value rules as the rest of Firstlight.

These are not claims that Mobile UI cannot build the corresponding interface. Firstlight supplies the reusable product contract so each consuming application does not need to design that contract independently.

## Richer contracts around familiar controls

Firstlight also provides opinionated versions of controls that have clear Mobile UI counterparts:

| Firstlight component | Additional Firstlight contract |
| --- | --- |
| **Segmented** | Stable string or integer values instead of renderer indexes, nullable selection, rich options, individual disabled choices, field metadata, strict diagnostics, and PHP-authoritative acceptance. |
| **Badge** | Exactly one count or label, hidden zero, contextual accessibility for numeric counts, five semantic tones, strict authoring diagnostics, and a Material 3 `Badge` on Android. |
| **Text Field** | A single semantic field API with content and autofill hints, platform icon overrides, accessible trailing actions, clear and reveal affordances, and focused editing reconciliation that preserves selection and text composition. |
| **Date Picker** | A strict nullable `YYYY-MM-DD` value, inclusive bound validation, a temporary native draft, explicit confirmation, and a closed trigger that continues to display PHP's accepted value. |
| **Select** | Stable string or integer values, rich and individually disabled options, automatic searchable presentation for larger collections, field validation semantics, and PHP-authoritative selection. |
| **Slider** | Strict finite-number and step-grid validation, helper and error treatment, an optional spoken accessibility value, and explicit live, blur, or debounce synchronisation. |
| **Switch** | Consistent helper and error semantics, strict Boolean values, one accessible setting row, and visible state reconciled from the value accepted by PHP. |

## Server-authoritative application state

For discrete Firstlight controls, a native interaction proposes a semantic value and PHP publishes the accepted state. PHP may accept, transform, or reject the proposal. Reconciliation updates the control without echoing another event, and programmatic updates never masquerade as user interaction.

This differs from treating a local optimistic change as accepted application state. It is useful when permissions, validation, dependent fields, or business rules can reject or replace a choice. Focused text and continuous gestures still retain the native draft state needed for responsive editing and movement; Firstlight applies the state model appropriate to each type of control.

## Consistency and diagnostics

Across the catalogue, Firstlight applies the same rules:

- selection binds stable domain strings or integers rather than display labels or renderer indexes;
- `null` consistently represents no selection;
- rich options can separate values, labels, and disabled state;
- malformed options, duplicate or mixed values, impossible ranges, contradictory props, and unsupported sync modes fail before publication;
- labels, helper text, errors, required metadata, accessibility hints, disabled state, and minimum interaction targets follow familiar conventions;
- the same authored component works on iOS and Android while each platform retains its native geometry, motion, presentation, and accessibility behaviour.

Firstlight deliberately exposes fewer visual escape hatches and platform-only options than a general-purpose primitive library. This narrower surface keeps application code portable and allows the components to behave consistently as the native platforms evolve.

## Laravel-shaped PHP extensions

Some Firstlight behaviour is not a new control. Field validation (`ValidatesFields`) runs Laravel's `Validator` in PHP and publishes the first `MessageBag` message into each field's existing `error` slot. Form submission (`SubmitsForms`) validates, runs a PHP callable once, and optionally sends success Feedback. Action authorization (`AuthorizesActions`) evaluates Laravel Gate/Policy decisions for hide, disable, and action-time guards. List pagination (`PaginatesLists`) binds Laravel paginators to List `@refresh` and `@endReached`. Destructive list actions (`DestroysListItems`) authorize Confirmation Dialog deletion by stable keys and republish `$listItems`. Package locale chrome publishes Firstlight-owned chrome strings from one Laravel language file, and Date/Time pickers inherit omitted locale and timezone from the application. Transient Feedback is an application-level outcome queue, not a Blade field. See [Validate fields](../how-to/validate-fields.md), [Submit forms](../how-to/submit-forms.md), [Authorize actions](../how-to/authorize-actions.md), [Paginate lists](../how-to/paginate-lists.md), [Destroy list items](../how-to/destroy-list-items.md), and [Localize chrome](../how-to/localize.md).

Layout, typography, and generic media stay in Mobile UI, and navigation chrome stays in NativePHP Mobile. Firstlight does not ship columns, bottom tabs, input masks, or a schema/form builder. Compose screens with Blade, Mobile UI layout, and Firstlight fields.

### Custom tappable content and accessibility

NativePHP core owns arbitrary-content `native:pressable` surfaces. In the supported
Mobile 4.6 implementation, Blade preserves their authored accessibility labels,
but the generic native renderers do not consume those labels/hints or explicitly
map a button role and disabled/selected state. Android's clickable supplies implicit
Compose grouping; iOS uses a tap gesture without explicit accessibility grouping.
Adding `a11y-label` to a `native:column` does not turn it into one accessible
measurement either. Do not assume a visual tap target is accessible.

Use [Button](../components/button.md) for labelled actions and
[List Item](../components/list-item.md) for application rows when their content
contracts fit. Use [Metric](../components/metric.md) for a static grouped statistic.
There is no supported arbitrary-content accessible action wrapper in Firstlight;
custom interactive banners need an upstream core accessibility fix. Panels,
dividers and tile grids remain Mobile UI layout, not catalogue controls.

## Reusing Mobile UI when it already fits

Firstlight does not maintain duplicate native code merely to put every control under its own namespace. **Button** and **Progress** currently keep public Firstlight element types while delegating directly to the official Mobile UI SwiftUI and Material 3 renderers.

Firstlight adds strict authoring boundaries, documentation, tests, and catalogue consistency around those primitives, but does not claim new native rendering functionality. If a durable cross-platform requirement later outgrows an adapter, Firstlight can introduce paired renderers without changing consumer markup. Generally useful improvements remain good candidates for contribution to Mobile UI itself.

## One native ecosystem

Firstlight components use ordinary NativePHP UI component extension points. They publish Element Tree data, receive standard semantic events, inherit Mobile UI theme tokens, and require no custom imperative bridge functions or WebView-backed control layer.

The relationship is intentionally complementary: **NativePHP provides the native foundation and chrome; Firstlight provides the app-shell layer of controls, Laravel contracts, and recipes on top of it.**

Review the current [compatibility requirements](../reference/compatibility.md) before releasing an application, particularly where server-authoritative controls depend on unchanged-tree publication acknowledgements from NativePHP Mobile.

--- Source: docs/concepts/accessibility.md ---

# Accessibility in Firstlight

Accessibility is a headline feature of Firstlight, and it starts with one
decision: every control is a real SwiftUI or Jetpack Compose control, not a
drawing that imitates one. VoiceOver, TalkBack, Dynamic Type, Android font
scaling, dark appearance, Increased Contrast, Reduce Motion, and right-to-left
layout reach each control the same way they reach the platform's own apps.

Firstlight then adds the parts a native control alone does not decide: whether
something has a name, how many focus stops a row has, how large a target is,
and what a screen reader hears when a form fails.

| Users who rely on | Get |
| --- | --- |
